opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the strangest results in the survey, and I don't think there's a fully satisfying explanation. Logically, if AI can do every task better and more cheaply than humans, you'd expect full automation of occupations to follow fairly soon after, or at least not decades later. But in our surveys, people give dates for high-level machine intelligence that are something like decades earlier than their dates for full automation of labor, sometimes with a gap of fifty or more years in the median forecasts.

I think a few things are probably going on. One is just framing effects. People answer differently depending on how a question is worded, and asking about "occupations" may call up a picture of jobs like surgeon or politician or childcare worker, where people imagine lots of social, legal, or preference-based reasons humans would still be doing them. Whereas "tasks" sounds more abstract and technical, so people think about capability rather than adoption.

Another possibility is that some respondents really are making a distinction between capability and deployment. Maybe they think that even once machines could do everything, there will be regulation, people wanting a human in the loop, slow institutional change, that sort of thing. That's a coherent view, though I'm skeptical it explains a gap that large.

But honestly, I suspect a lot of it is that people haven't thought about these questions very carefully, and they're giving fairly quick answers to hard questions. That's not a criticism exactly. These are busy researchers filling out a survey, and forecasting decades out is genuinely hard. But it does mean we should be cautious about treating any single number as a considered estimate. The inconsistency itself is informative: it tells you there's a lot of uncertainty and that the answers are sensitive to framing, which is a reason to look at the whole spread of responses rather than fixating on one median date.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes technical capability from deployment, suggesting respondents may forecast when AI can perform tasks separately from when occupations are actually automated.

r002.rationale: It says that if AI can do every task better and more cheaply, full automation of occupations should follow fairly soon.

r003.rationale: It does not say respondents were assigned to only one question or that this prevents comparing the same person’s answers.

r004.rationale: It notes a large gap between forecasts and calls the results inconsistent, but does not say the gap makes it likely that an individual would give inconsistent forecasts if asked both questions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the stranger findings, and honestly it's been there since the first time we ran the survey. We ask about two things that, on the face of it, should be roughly the same. One is high-level machine intelligence, which we define as machines being able to accomplish every task better and more cheaply than human workers, unaided. The other is full automation of labor, where every occupation is fully automatable. And people give wildly different answers. In the most recent survey, the median for high-level machine intelligence was somewhere around the late 2040s, and the median for full automation of labor was decades later, well into the next century.

Those really should be close, if not identical, because if you can do every task better than a human, then presumably you can do every occupation. So my first interpretation is just that people aren't thinking about this very carefully. These are long surveys, people are answering a lot of questions, and the framing is doing a lot of work. When you say "tasks," people picture things like writing code, proving theorems, driving. When you say "occupations," people picture a plumber, or a nurse, or a priest, and suddenly the whole embodied, social, institutional mess of a job comes into view. So it's partly that the word "occupation" is pulling in a bunch of stuff that "task" doesn't.

The second thing is that the occupation question is asked differently. We ask about specific occupations first, like truck driver, surgeon, retail salesperson, AI researcher, and then ask about full automation. So respondents have just been primed to think about all the particular jobs and how hard each one seems. The high-level machine intelligence question comes in more abstractly. I think that makes a real difference. The more concrete you get, the longer the timeline people give. We see this with a lot of questions, actually, which is a bit worrying for anyone wanting to take any of these numbers at face value.

And then there's a third possibility, which is that the gap is somewhat real. "Automatable" might mean something different to people than "could be done better." You might think a machine could do a surgeon's job better in some technical sense, but that it won't actually be deployed in that role for a long time because of regulation, or liability, or just people preferring a human. So full automation of labor is partly a forecast about society, not just about capabilities. That's a legitimate distinction, even if it probably doesn't explain a gap this large.

The honest takeaway for me is that these surveys tell you about how researchers are thinking as much as they tell you about the future. The specific numbers are noisy, and framing effects can shift things by decades. What I think you can still take from them is the broad picture: a large fraction of the field expects transformative capabilities within the careers of people working today, and a substantial chunk thinks that's risky. That part is pretty robust across framings. The precise year is not.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes technical ability from real-world deployment, citing regulation, liability, and preferences that could delay occupational automation.

r002.rationale: It says that if machines can do every task better than humans, they presumably can do every occupation.

r003.rationale: The response does not say respondents were assigned to only one question or that this prevents comparing an individual's answers.

r004.rationale: It describes a large difference between the medians, but does not suggest that an individual would give inconsistent forecasts if asked both questions.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a sign that we should be fairly cautious about interpreting these answers. You might think those are basically the same question, or that doing every task better than humans would be a stronger condition than being able to automate every occupation. So it’s somewhat surprising to get much earlier dates for the former.

One possibility is that people are distinguishing between having the capability and actually deploying it throughout the economy, which could take a long time. But if both questions are about what’s technically feasible, that doesn’t really resolve the discrepancy.

My guess is that the wording prompts people to think about different things. If you ask about high-level machine intelligence, they might think about the trajectory of AI research. If you ask about every occupation, they might start thinking about particular jobs and all the awkward things those involve. I don’t think we can tell from the answers alone exactly what’s happening, but it suggests these aren’t precise, stable forecasts that people already have in their heads.

r001.rationale: The response says respondents may distinguish technical capability from deploying automation throughout the economy, matching technical feasibility for high-level machine intelligence versus actual occupational adoption.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that automating every task implies automating occupations because occupations consist of tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not mention that asking different respondents only one question prevents detecting inconsistency within an individual's answers.

r004.rationale: It does not say the forecast gap suggests individuals would answer inconsistently if asked both questions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it is probably a framing effect. If you ask people when AI will be able to do every task better and more cheaply than humans, they seem to think about the general progress of AI. If you ask when every occupation will be fully automatable, they start thinking of particular occupations and all the awkward things those involve. You think, “Well, what about a plumber who has to go into somebody’s house?” And that can push the answer much later.

There is a real distinction between having the capability and actually deploying it everywhere. But if both questions are about what could be automated, rather than what actually will be, that doesn’t fully explain the gap. I’d take it as a warning that these answers are quite sensitive to how you ask the question, rather than interpreting them as a single, coherent forecast.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes capability from deployment, but does not clearly say respondents interpret the two questions as technical feasibility versus actual adoption.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that automating every task entails automating occupations because occupations are collections of tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss whether respondents answered only one question or the resulting inability to compare answers within individuals.

r004.rationale: It calls answers sensitive to framing, but does not say the gap makes an individual likely to give inconsistent forecasts when asked both questions.
